children: Lynas Rare Earths has agreed to buy Meteoric Resources in a deal that values the Australia-listed explorer at around US$672 million and gives Lynas a foothold in Brazil's growing rare-earths industry.

Under the all-share deal, Meteoric shareholders will get 0.0207 Lynas shares for each one in Meteoric they hold, the companies said in a joint statement Thursday. That implies an equity value of 968 million Australian dollars, or US$672.2 million, they said.
The deal represents a 68% premium to Meteoric's last close.

Meteoric owns the Caldeira rare earths project in the southwest region of Brazil's Minas Gerais state. The companies said the project is "the world's largest known ionic clay rare earth mineral resource outside China" reported in accordance with the JORC Code, the Australasian professional code for reporting exploration results, mineral resources and ore reserves.

Lynas has been expanding its business to capitalize on rising demand for rare earths produced outside of China, which dominates refining of the critical minerals. Rare earths, which are needed for electric vehicles and consumer electronics as well as jet fighters and missile systems, have been a key battleground amid trade tensions between the U.S. and China.

Lynas, which has a market value of nearly A$14 billion, is the biggest producer of separated rare earths outside of China. It is the only non-Chinese commercial producer of heavy rare earths, such as dysprosium and terbium, which are added to magnets to help them run more efficiently at higher temperatures.
Today, it has mining and processing operations in Australia and Malaysia.
Brazil is a well-established and supportive mining jurisdiction, and its rare-earth reserves are the largest outside China, said Lynas Chair John Humphrey.

"Expanding our operations into a new country will help Lynas maintain its leading position in the global rare-earths supply chain and meet increased customer demand for rare-earth materials," Humphrey said.

Lynas said the all-share structure of the deal ensures the company will be well placed to fund Caldeira and other growth projects. It expects the Caldeira project will cost more than US$500 million to develop.
Lynas will study the potential for additional downstream processing in Brazil, in line with the country's economic and sustainability goals, it said.
Meteoric Executive Chair Andrew Tunks said Caldeira is "an orebody that is high-grade, highly recoverable, low in capital intensity, low in operating cost, and highly scalable."

The Meteoric board unanimously recommended shareholders vote in favor of the takeover. Its directors, who together hold 2.6% of the company's stock, intend to vote for the deal, as does Meteoric's largest shareholder, investor Tolga Kumova, who has a roughly 6.7% stake, the companies said.
Meteoric shareholders will own roughly 5.9% of Lynas once the deal is completed, they said.
